stem: Draw the diagram of a sarcomere of skeletal muscle showing different regions.
solution:
A **sarcomere** is the portion of a myofibril between two successive **Z lines**; it is the functional unit of contraction (book figure attached: a sarcomere).

**Labels a marker looks for:**
1. **Z line**: an elastic fibre at each end of the sarcomere, bisecting the I band; the thin filaments are firmly attached to it.
2. **Thin (actin) filaments**: projecting inwards from each Z line, parallel to the long axis of the myofibril.
3. **Thick (myosin) filaments**: in the centre, parallel to the thin filaments, with projecting heads (cross arms).
4. **A band** (anisotropic, dark band): the length of the thick filaments, in the middle of the sarcomere.
5. **I band** (isotropic, light band): the region with thin filaments only; a sarcomere carries two half I bands, one at each end.
6. **H zone**: the central part of the A band, where the thick filaments are not overlapped by thin filaments.
7. **M line**: a thin fibrous membrane in the middle of the A band that holds the thick filaments together.
8. **Sarcomere**: bracketed from one Z line to the next.
groundedIn: §17.2; Fig. 17.2 — sarcomere between two successive Z lines; Z line bisects the I band, thin filaments attached to it; A band of thick filaments held by the M line; H zone not overlapped by thin filaments; two half I bands per sarcomere (stated in the chapter Summary)

stem: Define sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
solution:
The **sliding filament theory** states that contraction of a muscle fibre takes place by the **sliding of the thin (actin) filaments over the thick (myosin) filaments**.

The thin filaments are pulled towards the centre of the A band, the Z lines are pulled inwards and the sarcomere shortens: the **I bands get reduced** while the **A bands retain their length**.
groundedIn: §17.2.2; Fig. 17.5 — contraction of a muscle fibre takes place by the sliding of the thin filaments over the thick filaments; I bands reduced, A bands retain length

stem: Describe the important steps in muscle contraction.
solution:
Muscle contraction takes place by the **sliding of thin filaments over thick filaments**, in the following steps:

1. **Neural signal:** a signal from the **CNS** reaches the muscle fibre through a **motor neuron**.
2. **Neuromuscular junction:** at the **motor-end plate** the signal releases the neurotransmitter **acetylcholine**, which generates an **action potential** in the sarcolemma.
3. **Release of calcium:** the action potential spreads through the muscle fibre and causes the release of \(\text{Ca}^{++}\) from the **sarcoplasmic reticulum** into the sarcoplasm.
4. **Unmasking of actin:** \(\text{Ca}^{++}\) binds to a subunit of **troponin** on the actin filaments and removes the masking of the active sites for myosin.
5. **Cross bridge formation:** using energy from **ATP hydrolysis**, the myosin head binds to the exposed active sites on actin, forming a **cross bridge**.
6. **Sliding:** the cross bridge pulls the actin filaments towards the centre of the A band; the Z lines are pulled inwards and the **sarcomere shortens** (contraction). The I bands get reduced; the A bands retain their length.
7. **Breaking of the cross bridge:** myosin releases ADP and \(\text{P}_\text{i}\) and returns to its relaxed state; a new ATP binds and the cross bridge is broken. ATP is hydrolysed again and the cycle repeats, causing further sliding.
8. **Relaxation:** when \(\text{Ca}^{++}\) is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic cisternae, the actin filaments are masked again and the Z lines return to their original position.
groundedIn: §17.2.2; §17.2.1; Fig. 17.4; Fig. 17.5 — motor neuron, motor-end plate, acetyl choline, action potential, Ca++ release, troponin unmasking, cross bridge formation using ATP, sliding towards centre of A band, cross bridge breaking, Ca++ pumped back causing relaxation

context: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true.
stem: Actin is present in thin filament
solution: **True.** Actin filaments are thinner than myosin filaments and are called **thin filaments**. Each thin filament is made of two **F (filamentous) actins** helically wound to each other, with tropomyosin and troponin.
groundedIn: §17.2; §17.2.1 — actin filaments are thinner and called thin filaments; each actin (thin) filament is made of two F actins helically wound

context: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true.
stem: H-zone of striated muscle fibre represents both thick and thin filaments.
solution:
**False.** The **H zone** is the central part of the thick filaments that is **not overlapped by thin filaments**.

Corrected statement: H-zone of striated muscle fibre represents only thick filaments.
groundedIn: §17.2; Fig. 17.2 — the central part of thick filament, not overlapped by thin filaments, is called the H zone

context: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true.
stem: Human skeleton has 206 bones.
solution: **True.** In human beings the skeletal system is made up of **206 bones** and a few cartilages; 80 of these form the axial skeleton and the rest form the appendicular skeleton.
groundedIn: §17.3 — in human beings this system is made up of 206 bones and a few cartilages; axial skeleton comprises 80 bones

context: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true.
stem: There are 11 pairs of ribs in man.
solution:
**False.** Man has **12 pairs of ribs**: 7 pairs of true ribs, 3 pairs (8th, 9th and 10th) of vertebrochondral (false) ribs and 2 pairs (11th and 12th) of floating ribs.

Corrected statement: There are 12 pairs of ribs in man.
groundedIn: §17.3; Fig. 17.8 — there are 12 pairs of ribs; true, vertebrochondral (false) and floating ribs

context: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true.
stem: Sternum is present on the ventral side of the body.
solution: **True.** The **sternum** is a flat bone on the **ventral midline of the thorax**; the true ribs are connected ventrally to it.
groundedIn: §17.3 — sternum is a flat bone on the ventral midline of thorax; ribs connected ventrally to the sternum

context: Write the difference between :
stem: Actin and Myosin
solution:
| Basis of difference | Actin | Myosin |
|---|---|---|
| Type of filament | **Thin filament** | **Thick filament** |
| Band | Present in the light **I band** (isotropic band) | Present in the dark **A band** (anisotropic band) |
| Attachment | Firmly attached to the **Z line** | Held together in the middle of the A band by the **M line** |
| Structure | Two **F actins** helically wound; each F actin is a polymer of monomeric **G actins** | A polymer of many monomeric proteins called **meromyosins** |
| Associated proteins / parts | **Tropomyosin** and **troponin** run along it | Each meromyosin has a globular head with a short arm (**HMM**) and a tail (**LMM**) |
| Active sites | Has active binding sites for myosin, masked by troponin at rest | Head is an **ATPase** with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin |
| Role in contraction | Slides towards the centre of the A band | Heads form cross bridges and pull the actin filaments |
groundedIn: §17.2; §17.2.1; §17.2.2 — thin and thick filaments; I band contains actin, A band myosin; Z line and M line; F and G actins, tropomyosin, troponin; meromyosin HMM and LMM; ATPase head; cross bridges pull actin towards centre of A band

context: Write the difference between :
stem: Red and White muscles
solution:
| Basis of difference | Red muscle fibres | White muscle fibres |
|---|---|---|
| Myoglobin | Content **high** | Very less quantity |
| Colour | Reddish appearance | Pale or whitish |
| Mitochondria | Plenty | Few |
| Sarcoplasmic reticulum | Less | Amount is **high** |
| Source of energy | Use the large amount of oxygen stored in them for ATP production, so called **aerobic muscles** | Depend on the **anaerobic process** for energy |
groundedIn: §17.2.2 — red fibres: high myoglobin, plenty of mitochondria, aerobic muscles; white fibres: very less myoglobin, few mitochondria, high sarcoplasmic reticulum, depend on anaerobic process

context: Write the difference between :
stem: Pectoral and Pelvic girdle
solution:
| Basis of difference | Pectoral girdle | Pelvic girdle |
|---|---|---|
| Limb articulated | Helps in articulation of the **upper limb** (fore limb) with the axial skeleton | Helps in articulation of the **lower limb** (hind limb) with the axial skeleton |
| Each half | Consists of a **clavicle** and a **scapula** | Consists of one **coxal bone**, formed by the fusion of **ilium, ischium and pubis** |
| Cavity for the limb bone | **Glenoid cavity** (below the acromion of the scapula) articulates with the head of the **humerus** to form the shoulder joint | **Acetabulum** (at the point of fusion of the three bones) articulates with the thigh bone (**femur**) |
| Pubic symphysis | Absent | The two halves meet ventrally to form the **pubic symphysis**, containing fibrous cartilage |
groundedIn: §17.3; Fig. 17.9; Fig. 17.10 — pectoral and pelvic girdles articulate upper and lower limbs; clavicle and scapula; glenoid cavity and shoulder joint; coxal bone of ilium, ischium and pubis; acetabulum; pubic symphysis

stem:
Match Column I with Column II :

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) Smooth muscle | (i) Myoglobin |
| (b) Tropomyosin | (ii) Thin filament |
| (c) Red muscle | (iii) Sutures |
| (d) Skull | (iv) Involuntary |
solution:
(a) - (iv), (b) - (ii), (c) - (i), (d) - (iii)

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) Smooth muscle | (iv) Involuntary |
| (b) Tropomyosin | (ii) Thin filament |
| (c) Red muscle | (i) Myoglobin |
| (d) Skull | (iii) Sutures |

- **Smooth (visceral) muscles** are not under the voluntary control of the nervous system, so they are involuntary.
- Two filaments of **tropomyosin** run close to the F actins of the thin filament.
- **Red muscle** fibres have a high content of myoglobin.
- The flat **skull** bones fuse end-to-end through **sutures** (fibrous joints) to form the cranium.
groundedIn: §17.2; §17.2.1; §17.2.2; §17.4 — visceral muscles are involuntary; tropomyosin runs along the F actins of the thin filament; red fibres high in myoglobin; flat skull bones fuse by sutures

stem: What are the different types of movements exhibited by the cells of human body?
solution:
Cells of the human body exhibit three main types of movement: **amoeboid**, **ciliary** and **muscular**.

1. **Amoeboid movement:** shown by specialised cells such as **macrophages and leucocytes** in blood. It is effected by **pseudopodia** formed by the streaming of protoplasm; cytoskeletal elements like microfilaments are also involved.
2. **Ciliary movement:** occurs in most internal tubular organs lined by **ciliated epithelium**. Coordinated movements of cilia in the **trachea** remove dust particles and foreign substances inhaled with air; ciliary movement also helps the passage of **ova through the female reproductive tract**.
3. **Muscular movement:** movement of the **limbs, jaws, tongue**, etc., uses the contractile property of muscles; it is used for locomotion and other movements.
groundedIn: §17.1 — amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movements; macrophages and leucocytes, pseudopodia, microfilaments; ciliated epithelium of trachea, passage of ova; limbs, jaws, tongue need muscular movement

stem: How do you distinguish between a skeletal muscle and a cardiac muscle?
solution:
| Basis of difference | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Closely associated with the **skeletal components** of the body | Muscle of the **heart** |
| Control | **Voluntary**: under the voluntary control of the nervous system | **Involuntary**: the nervous system does not control its activities directly |
| Arrangement | Muscle fibres grouped into bundles (**fascicles**) held together by **fascia**; each fibre is a multinucleate syncitium | Many cardiac muscle cells assemble in a **branching pattern** |
| Function | Locomotory actions and changes of body posture | Contraction of the heart |

Both are **striated** in appearance.
groundedIn: §17.2; Fig. 17.1 — skeletal muscles associated with skeletal components, striated, voluntary, locomotion and posture; muscle bundles (fascicles) held by fascia, fibre a syncitium; cardiac muscles of heart, branching pattern, striated, involuntary

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: atlas/axis
solution: **Pivot joint**: a synovial joint, between the atlas and the axis.
groundedIn: §17.4 — pivot joint (between atlas and axis), a synovial joint

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: carpal/metacarpal of thumb
solution: **Saddle joint**: a synovial joint, between the carpal and the metacarpal of the thumb.
groundedIn: §17.4 — saddle joint (between carpal and metacarpal of thumb), a synovial joint

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: between phalanges
solution: **Hinge joint**: a synovial joint (the interphalangeal joints), like the knee joint.
groundedIn: §17.4 — hinge joint (knee joint) is a synovial joint; BEYOND CHAPTER: the joints between phalanges (interphalangeal joints) are hinge joints

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: femur/acetabulum
solution: **Ball and socket joint**: a synovial joint, formed where the head of the femur (thigh bone) articulates with the acetabulum of the coxal bone.
groundedIn: §17.3; §17.4 — acetabulum is the cavity to which the thigh bone articulates; ball and socket joint is a synovial joint; BEYOND CHAPTER: the femur/acetabulum (hip) joint is a ball and socket joint

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: between cranial bones
solution: **Fibrous joint** (sutures): the flat skull bones fuse end-to-end through dense fibrous connective tissue to form the cranium; it allows no movement.
groundedIn: §17.4 — fibrous joints do not allow any movement; flat skull bones fuse end-to-end in the form of sutures to form the cranium

context: Name the type of joint between the following:-
stem: between pubic bones in the pelvic girdle
solution: **Cartilaginous joint** (pubic symphysis): the two halves of the pelvic girdle meet ventrally and are joined by fibrous cartilage.
groundedIn: §17.3; §17.4 — the two halves of the pelvic girdle meet ventrally to form the pubic symphysis containing fibrous cartilage; in cartilaginous joints bones are joined together with the help of cartilages

In a muscle fibre \(\text{Ca}^{++}\) is stored in the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**.
